findings.title: Failed device-limit writes are cached, allowing the limit to be bypassed
findings.body: tagDeviceUI stores the device ID in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice propagates the error and the first anonymous authentication fails, but the cache entry remains. For the cache TTL (29 minutes), subsequent requests with the same device ID return nil from tagDeviceUI without checking the limit or persisting the device, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. This allows a device rejected by the limit to access anonymously and makes the limit ineffective. Cache only after successful persistence or delete the cache entry on error.

findings.title: Device limit check and insert are not atomic
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs a separate COUNT(*) to check the active-device limit and then runs the upsert in another session without a transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from distinct new device IDs can both observe count < device_limit and then insert, exceeding the configured limit. If device_limit is intended as a hard bound, enforce it atomically (for example with a conditional insert/update, transactional locking, or a database constraint/trigger).

findings.title: COUNT query is executed in the authentication path when the limit is enabled
findings.body: When device_limit is greater than zero, every anonymous request that misses the local cache runs COUNT(*) over anon_device during authentication before upserting. On instances with many anonymous devices, this can add latency and database load. Consider a cheaper enforcement strategy, such as an approximate cached counter or a conditional write that avoids a separate count query.

findings.title: No tests cover device-limit failures through TagDevice/authentication
findings.body: The added store test checks that a second device is rejected when the limit is 1, but there is no service-level test for TagDevice with a configured AnonymousDeviceLimit. In particular, nothing verifies that a limit-reached error blocks anonymous authentication and that a failed write is not cached, which is the interaction that allows the limit to be bypassed. Add integration tests with a non-zero device limit and repeated requests for the same device ID.
